# Git Worktree Workflows for AI-Assisted Development

Git worktrees allow multiple working directories to share a single repository. Introduced in Git 2.5 (2015), they became newly relevant when AI coding agents created a need for fast, lightweight isolation across parallel tasks. As of early 2026, Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot CLI all ship native worktree support for parallel agent execution.

This research examines how worktrees work, how AI tools use them, what patterns have emerged, and where the approach breaks down — with every claim traced to a web source visited in-session.

## Key Findings

| Dimension | Finding |
|-----------|---------|
| Tool adoption | Claude Code (`--worktree`), Cursor (automatic), and Copilot CLI (mode selection) all use worktrees; Aider, OpenHands, and Devin do not |
| Practical scale | 3-5 parallel agents is the observed ceiling before coordination overhead dominates |
| Biggest gap | Worktrees isolate files but **not** databases, ports, or Docker — runtime isolation requires hooks or external tooling |
| Code quality | AI-authored PRs produce 1.7× more issues than human-only PRs (CodeRabbit, n=470) |
| Conflict prevention | Single-writer rule + additive-only changes + merge-early-and-often |
| Disk optimization | pnpm content-addressable store reduces Node.js dependency duplication by ~63% |
| Known risk | Concurrent git operations across worktrees can corrupt shared .git data |

## Decision Framework

1. **Multiple parallel agents on independent tasks** → use worktrees
2. **Application uses databases/ports/services** → add WorktreeCreate hooks for per-worktree isolation
3. **Need complete isolation (no shared state)** → use full clones
4. **Conflict-free single-user editing** → consider GitButler virtual branches
5. **Sequential dependent changes** → use stacked diffs (Graphite), optionally combine with worktrees
6. **Full environment isolation required** → use containers/devcontainers
